My approach to branding

A good identity
has reasons behind it.

Before choosing a typeface, I want to understand the business. Who needs it? What do they care about? What should they understand when they find it?

Start with what is true.

The most useful part of brand strategy is deciding what deserves to lead. A business may have ten things to say. The person meeting it for the first time needs somewhere to begin.

I look for the thing that makes the offer clear and the details that make it believable. Those become the foundation for the positioning, the voice and the visual direction.

Make the choices work together.

Colour can set a mood. Type can give a name presence. A sentence can make a complicated offer feel straightforward. Each choice should help the others do their job.

For Sapentine, “Above and underfoot” connects the service range. For Proficient, the light symbol makes the trade clear. For Kepti, everyday language makes the product feel closer to the working day. Different businesses need different answers.

Think past the presentation.

A brand kit should be useful after the first look. Can the identity work on a phone? Is the message clear on a service page? Does the person posting next week know which colours, words and layouts to use?

That is why I include application guidance, voice examples and practical rules alongside the visual direction. They give the next decision somewhere to start.

Keep the words in the room.

I write as I think through the identity. A headline often reveals whether the positioning is clear. An enquiry prompt reveals whether the next step makes sense. The visual work and the copy get stronger when they develop together.
